## What this letter says
One doctor wrote this letter to another doctor. It is about you. The doctor will see you soon.

You have Wilson's disease. You learned this at age 14. You take penicillamine for it.

You went to a hospital in Randolph, North Carolina. You were short of breath. Your heart raced (palpitations). Your chest felt uncomfortable. Doctors found atrial fibrillation with a fast rate.

Your heartbeat went back to normal on its own (normal sinus rhythm). You needed no more treatment for it.

A heart scan (echocardiogram) showed:
- mild-to-moderate left atrial enlargement
- a normal ejection fraction
- no other significant valve problem

In North Carolina, you said you had cirrhosis from Wilson's disease. A liver specialist said to avoid Coumadin. The reason was questionable significant liver disease.

You have never had a liver biopsy. So the cirrhosis diagnosis is in doubt. The letter says your liver disease status is unclear.

Your liver function tests (LFTs) have stayed normal. Your copper level has been undetectable on your dose of penicillamine.

Your heartbeat was normal when the writing doctor saw you on 06/12/2008. You take metoprolol and aspirin without any difficulty.

The atrial fibrillation may come and go (potentially paroxysmal). The enlarged left atrium could raise your risk of it coming back.

The writing doctor wants advice on two things:
- long-term anticoagulation
- rhythm control

The letter does not say if Coumadin will be started.

## What you need to do
1. The letter does not ask you to do anything.

## Dates and medicines
Date: 06/12/2008. The writing doctor saw you. The letter does not make clear if this is 6 December or 12 June.

The letter does not say when the atrial fibrillation happened.

Medicines:
- Penicillamine: 250 milligrams by mouth, four times a day.
- Metoprolol: 12.5 milligrams, twice a day. You started Lopressor in North Carolina. You tolerated it well.
- Aspirin: 325 milligrams, once a day. You got aspirin in North Carolina instead of Coumadin.

## Questions to ask your doctor
1. Will I need Coumadin?
2. What does my liver status mean for my treatment?
3. What can be done about my heart rhythm?

## When to get urgent help
The letter does not list specific warning signs.

If you are worried and it is not an emergency, call NHS 111. In an emergency, call 999.

---
*This explanation was made by a computer program to help you read your letter. It may contain mistakes. It does not replace your doctor, nurse or pharmacist. Always follow the letter and ask them if anything is unclear.*
